default.p.55new_n3-t1-p1.outline.0.note: Introduces the custom of children receiving New Year's money and the idea of an appropriate amount for young children.
default.p.55new_n3-t1-p1.outline.1.label: The usual amount of New Year's money
default.p.55new_n3-t1-p1.outline.1.note: Statistics on common New Year's gift-money amounts by school level, from elementary school through high school.
default.p.55new_n3-t1-p1.outline.2.label: The Yamada family's rules for giving New Year's money

default.p.55new_n3-t1-p1.vietnamese:
Many children receive New Year’s gift money.

We may give that much to the children of people who have helped us, but we object to giving too much money to young children.

Many people give 2,000 yen to first- through third-grade elementary school students, 3,000 yen to fourth- through sixth-graders, 5,000 yen to junior high school students, and 5,000 or 10,000 yen to high school students.

Mr. Yamada lives with his son.

Mr. Yamada gives first-graders 1,000 yen and second-graders 2,000 yen, increasing the amount by 1,000 yen each year.

Mr. Yamada’s son gives 3,000 yen to children from first through third grade, 5,000 yen to children from fourth grade through junior high school, and 10,000 yen to high school students and above.

default.p.55new_n3-t10-p1.vietnamese:
In Japan, lucky bags sell very well around New Year's.

Although it is impossible to see the merchandise inside a lucky bag, they are popular because they offer a great bargain.

For example, a 1,000-yen lucky bag usually contains items worth around 2,000 yen in total.

As a result, some people even line up the day before to buy one.

People do not mind even if the bag contains items they do not need.

Some people immediately take the items out of the bag and exchange them on the spot.

Moreover, nowadays they can be resold online, so buyers ultimately always make a profit.

default.p.55new_n3-t11-p1.outline.0.note: Begins by introducing the popular Mazui-bō snack and its similarity in name to famous types of candy.
default.p.55new_n3-t11-p1.outline.1.label: The origin and meaning of the name 「Mazui」
default.p.55new_n3-t11-p1.outline.1.note: Explains the reason for the name: the bread is not bad; rather, the company’s business situation is poor. This is a pun based on the multiple meanings of mazui. The passage contains the basis for Question 1.
default.p.55new_n3-t11-p1.outline.2.label: The attention-grabbing effect and the lesson about product names
default.p.55new_n3-t11-p1.outline.2.note: Describes the positive results of choosing an unusual name, which attracted attention and led to strong sales, concluding that product names are important. This passage contains the basis for Question 2.
default.p.55new_n3-t11-p1.vietnamese:
The snack 「Mazui-bō」 (Bad Stick) is selling very well.

This snack is similar to the famous snacks called 「Umai-bō」 and 「Umaka-bō」.

Why does it have such a name?

It does not mean that the snack tastes bad.

The snack is not bad at all.

The package says that the "bad" thing is the company's business situation.

In addition to meaning "not tasty," 「Mazui」 can also mean "not good" or "not okay."

By naming the product 「Mazui」, the company attracted attention from the outset, prompting reactions such as "What is this?", "How interesting!", and "Are they really selling something bad?" As a result, it sold very well.

It is clear that a product's name is extremely important.

default.p.55new_n3-t12-p1.vietnamese:
In business, people are taught that the rule "①Hourensou" is important.

This is formed from the first kanji of "reporting, contacting, and discussing."

It is said to be what subordinates should do for their superiors.

Then, what should superiors do for their subordinates?

It is said that the rule "②Ohitashi" is best.

It means "O: do not get angry, Hi: do not deny, Ta: help, Shi: give instructions/guidance."

Both are necessary, but it would be wonderful, especially, if people could put ② into practice.

I went with my two children, three people in total, to a ramen restaurant famous for its delicious food.

I wanted to order three bowls of “chashu ramen” for 700 yen each, but because I did not have enough money, I chose a 500-yen bowl of shoyu ramen instead.

I did not know that the restaurant accepted cash only.

After paying, I had exactly 100 yen left in my wallet.

There are still stores in Japan that do not accept payment cards.

default.p.55new_n3-t14-p1.outline.0.note: Notes that the number of people who do not read newspapers is increasing, while young people believe there is no need to pay for newspapers because the Internet is available.
default.p.55new_n3-t14-p1.outline.1.label: The limitations of reading news on the Internet
default.p.55new_n3-t14-p1.outline.1.note: Points out that a drawback of reading online is that people only skim headlines and end up reading only what interests them. Main evidence for Question 2.
default.p.55new_n3-t14-p1.outline.2.label: The outstanding advantages of print newspapers
default.p.55new_n3-t14-p1.outline.2.note: Points out the advantage of printed newspapers: simply opening one or skimming it allows readers to take in a wide variety of information.
default.p.55new_n3-t14-p1.outline.3.label: The author’s wishes and concerns
default.p.55new_n3-t14-p1.outline.3.note: The author wants people to read more newspapers because having broad knowledge of current information is most important, while expressing concern that continuing to read only according to personal preferences may become a problem.
default.p.55new_n3-t14-p1.vietnamese:
The number of people who do not read newspapers is steadily increasing.

Since news can also be read on the Internet, young people in particular say that there is no need to pay to read newspapers.

However, online, people only see the headlines and choose to read articles from among a small number of them.

As a result, they read only the content that interests them.

With a printed newspaper, you can learn many things simply by opening it.

Even a quick glance can provide a great deal of information.

I want more people to read newspapers.

That is because I think the most important thing is to learn about information in the first place.

It is worrying if things continue this way.

default.p.55new_n3-t15-p1.outline.0.note: Introduces coffee’s immediate effects and analyzes its long-term benefits for the heart and brain and its role in reducing the risk of dementia. The basis for Question 2 is in Sentence 1.
default.p.55new_n3-t15-p1.outline.1.label: The optimal timing and method for drinking coffee

default.p.55new_n3-t15-p1.outline.2.label: A warning against excessive coffee consumption
default.p.55new_n3-t15-p1.outline.2.note: Transition warning that drinking more is not always better; drinking five cups or more has the opposite effect. The basis for Question 1 is Sentence 5.
default.p.55new_n3-t15-p1.vietnamese:
Many people say that when they feel sleepy, drinking coffee helps them feel more alert.

default.p.55new_n3-t21-p1.vietnamese:
Normally, filtered water or hot water comes out of faucets, but at most elementary and junior high schools in Shizuoka Prefecture, which is famous as a tea-producing region, tea comes out instead.

The city of Shimada started this initiative in the hope that students would develop a love of tea, and it is reportedly planned to be installed at all elementary and junior high schools throughout Shizuoka Prefecture.

Shizuoka Prefecture is not the only place where something unusual comes out of a faucet. At Kagawa Prefecture's airport, reportedly, dashi broth also comes out of one.

Kagawa Prefecture is famous for udon noodles. They offer the udon broth free of charge.

However, because the daily quantity is limited, it is sometimes unavailable.

Udon restaurants started this initiative to promote Kagawa's udon noodles.

Because the broth is delicious, it is highly praised by visitors, and it has apparently also sparked their interest in udon noodles.

Therefore, it can be said to be fulfilling its role very well.

In addition, faucets dispensing mandarin juice, peach juice, Calpis, and so on are also being created.

What an interesting idea!

default.p.55new_n3-t22-p1.outline.1.note: Describes the spread of literacy through terakoya schools in the Edo period, literacy-rate figures from the beginning of the Meiji period, and how literacy was crucial for learning Western culture and technology. Contains evidence for Question 2.

default.p.55new_n3-t22-p1.vietnamese:
Before Chinese characters were introduced from China, Japan had no writing system, so people always had to meet others in person whenever they wanted to communicate something.

As a result, it must have taken a long time for information to reach many people, and there must also have been many cases in which information was distorted as it was passed on.

Later, after adopting Chinese characters and creating katakana and hiragana, Japanese people’s lives became more convenient.

During the Edo period (1603–1867), children from ordinary families often attended terakoya schools to learn to read and write.

According to the author Dore, in the first year of the Meiji period (1868), Japan’s literacy rate was 43% among men and 10% among women.

Some people believe that the rates were actually higher, but whether those figures were large or small is not the key issue.

What matters is that a considerable number of people could read and write. In fact, this greatly helped Japan absorb Western culture and technology during the Meiji period (1868–1912).

However, in the 21st century, the amount of educational expenditure covered by the Japanese government is very small compared with that of other developed countries.

As a result, children from economically disadvantaged families have difficulty accessing higher education.

If this situation continues, it is deeply concerning for Japan’s future.

default.p.55new_n3-t23-p1.vietnamese:
I watched a secretly filmed video of someone giving a homeless man $100 to see what he would use the money for.

I was very surprised to see him use the money to buy food and then begin distributing it to other homeless people in the park.

If he had used it only for himself, he probably would not have had to worry about food for several days.

When asked why he did it, he replied, “Whenever I see another person’s happy face, I feel happy too.”

I was even more surprised when I learned that the homeless people in the park were strangers to him.

① I thought that human beings really are wonderful and good.

I heard that one reason he became homeless was that he had to quit his job to care for his wife’s sick father.

Apparently, he became homeless even though it was certainly not simply because he was lazy.

He said that many people are in circumstances similar to his.

When I told my husband this story, he said that it was probably precisely because he was the kind of person he was that he became homeless.

② It was truly a video that made me think deeply.

default.p.55new_n3-t24-p1.vietnamese:
Foreigners seem shocked when they see that Japanese elementary school children walk to and from school entirely on their own.

In many countries, adults take children to school and pick them up afterward.

Therefore, when a video of a first-grade girl taking the train to school alone for the first time was broadcast, the entire world was astonished.

There were both approving and opposing opinions.

For Japanese people, however, it is natural and ordinary.

①Because they themselves did the same thing in the past.

Japan may be safe enough for children to do this.

Even so, children today are different from children in the past in that, for example, they are expected to go straight home after school.

I remember that when I was young, school ended at 4:30 p.m. in winter and around 5:00 p.m. in summer, and until then we were allowed to play in the schoolyard.

Nowadays, however, children are told to go home early and are required to leave the school grounds immediately (that is, this is what happens).

Even so, because they are only with other children, they can still play a little or chat on the way home, enjoying ②some relaxed time.

That will surely be a time they look back on nostalgically when they grow up.

default.p.55new_n3-t25-p1.outline.1.note: Although criticized as a waste of tax money, the local manhole covers are very popular; manhole cards distributed free of charge since 2016 are even sought after and resold.
default.p.55new_n3-t25-p1.outline.2.label: The tourism benefits and English name of manhole covers
default.p.55new_n3-t25-p1.outline.2.note: Tourist-attracting manhole covers benefit tourism, prompting Sendai to create English-language manhole covers; the trend may spread to other places.
default.p.55new_n3-t25-p1.vietnamese:
A manhole cover is a cover placed over access points to sewer drainage pipes or gas pipes.

In Japan, some manhole covers are designed with flowers, animals, or, more recently, famous local landmarks.

The inexpensive ones cost only about ¥1,000, but designed covers cost around ¥60,000, and colored covers can reportedly cost as much as ¥100,000.

Although they are sometimes criticized as a waste of taxpayers' money, uniquely designed local manhole covers are now very popular, even though they account for only about 10% of all manhole covers.

Since 2016, when manhole cards began being distributed throughout Japan, their popularity has increased even further.

More than one million cards have been distributed free of charge so far, but some cards are even sold (that is how popular they are).

People gather in large numbers to collect the cards or admire the manhole covers.

This is also very beneficial for tourism.

For this reason, Sendai City has reportedly even produced manhole covers with English text.

I have a feeling that English manhole covers will also become more common in other places from now on.

default.p.55new_n3-t26-p1.outline.1.note: A real-life example: when someone gets lost in Osaka, a person may proactively approach them, ask if they need help, and actively look for someone who can assist. Basis for Question 1.

default.p.55new_n3-t26-p1.outline.2.note: Compared with Tokyo, people in Tokyo are not necessarily rude but are often too busy to stop and help; one must actively ask them for assistance. Evidence for Question 3.
default.p.55new_n3-t26-p1.outline.3.label: Osaka’s open personality and love of laughter
default.p.55new_n3-t26-p1.outline.3.note: People in Osaka are willing to start conversations with strangers and respond cheerfully to humorous actions. This supports question 4.
default.p.55new_n3-t26-p1.outline.4.label: Conclusion: places where people care about others are easier to live in
default.p.55new_n3-t26-p1.outline.4.note: The main reason given for recommending life in Osaka is that places where many people care about their surroundings are the easiest places to live. This is the basis for Question 2.
default.p.55new_n3-t26-p1.vietnamese:
I was born, raised, and still live in Tokyo, so I know many good things about Tokyo. Nevertheless, I would like to tell foreigners that Osaka is a better place to live.

The food being both inexpensive and delicious is one reason, but mainly because I think people in Osaka have a stronger spirit of hospitality.

In Osaka, if you are lost, someone will immediately ask you questions such as, “Where are you trying to go?”

Even if that person does not know, they will ask someone else for help, saying, “Does anyone know where this place is?”

This does not mean that people in Tokyo are unkind, but in Tokyo you have to take the initiative and ask first.

In Tokyo, many people simply walk past even when they notice someone needs help. This may be partly because they are busy.

In addition, people in Osaka often start conversations with complete strangers.

Even when the person making a joke is someone they do not know, they accept it and laugh along.

And then lively laughter rings out.

Of course, not everyone behaves this way, and unpleasant people can be found anywhere, but I think it is easier to live in a place where many people are always considerate of those around them.

default.p.55new_n3-t27-p1.vietnamese:
At restaurants such as sushi and tempura restaurants, diners seated at the counter can watch the cooking.

It is interesting to watch the dishes gradually being completed, and diners can also chat with the chef.

Apparently, people from countries without restaurants of this kind find the experience very exciting.

Therefore, it is not surprising that a restaurant would open specifically to provide foreign guests with this experience.

Diners eat while watching top chefs prepare food in a kitchen designed like a stage.

It feels exactly like watching a performance.

Because translation services are available in 20 languages, foreigners who do not understand Japanese can also fully enjoy the experience.

The restaurant serves a set menu combining cuisines from several countries, centered on Japanese food.

Including the service charge, the price is 15,000 yen, with a little change still left over (although some dishes are expensive), so it is sure to be popular with foreign guests.

default.p.55new_n3-t28-p1.vietnamese:
Generally, magazines sell well when they contain interesting content.

However, among them are some women's magazines whose content seems completely unrelated to their sales.

People buy them because they want the free gifts included with them, so the magazines quickly sell out.

This is because they come with items such as handbags or cosmetics from famous brands.

Some companies sell magazines for preschool children in the same way.

They include kits for making toys that children enjoy.

The products receive excellent feedback because children can make small toys that look exactly like real machines.

This also delights adults.

That is because making them is difficult, and preschool children cannot manage to do it by themselves.

For example, the 「coin drop」game looks very similar to a machine in an arcade.

It is a game in which coins are dropped in from outside to make the stacked coins fall and collect them.

Once completed, the toy operates exactly like the machine in an arcade.

That is why children love it too.

default.p.55new_n3-t3-p1.vietnamese:
The last train I can take home departs at 24:44.

If I miss it, I use an overnight express bus that costs 1,340 yen.

It departs very late, at 25:30, but because the seats are reserved, there are times when I cannot get on the bus.

If I take a taxi, I can get home at any time, but it costs about 7,500 yen.

Therefore, when I do not have any money, it is better to go to an internet café.

For about 2,000 yen, many places include a shower room, which is very convenient.

default.p.55new_n3-t30-p1.vietnamese:
In countries such as China and the United States, there are “rage rooms,” where people can vent their anger by smashing televisions, furniture, bottles, and other items.

In everyday life, people are usually told not to break things, but in these rooms, they can use baseball bats or hammers to smash objects.

Because dangerous fragments may fly around, participants wear special protective clothing, helmets, and face coverings that completely conceal their faces.

Some people even bring their own belongings to smash.

Apparently, smashing things there relieves all their stress.

In China, for about 23 dollars, people can smash things continuously for 30 minutes.

Apparently, about 600 people visit each month, and approximately 15,000 bottles are smashed.

If so many people are this stressed, perhaps modern society is difficult for everyone to live in.

In the video, the room is filled with piles of broken bottles and damaged furniture.

They probably felt relieved and refreshed after smashing things.

The girl who comes out of the room is smiling.

It seems that rooms like this will eventually appear in Japan as well.

No, perhaps the appearance of such rooms will not be limited to Japan alone.

default.p.55new_n3-t31-p1.outline.0.label: The concept of homelessness
default.p.55new_n3-t31-p1.outline.0.note: Begins by defining the fixed residences of homeless people, such as tents in parks or along rivers because they lack money.
default.p.55new_n3-t31-p1.outline.1.label: The emergence and reasons for Address Hopper
default.p.55new_n3-t31-p1.outline.1.note: Shifts to people with money who sleep in a different place every day, known as Address Hoppers, and gives two main reasons: lower costs and many unexpected, interesting encounters. This supports Questions 2 and 3.
default.p.55new_n3-t31-p1.outline.2.label: The practical lifestyle of an Address Hopper
default.p.55new_n3-t31-p1.outline.2.note: Describes living like a tourist: using only one backpack, staying in homestays or share houses, using rental, laundry, and storage services, and having an official address without actually living there. Evidence for Question 1.
default.p.55new_n3-t31-p1.outline.3.label: Comments and evaluation of this lifestyle
default.p.55new_n3-t31-p1.outline.3.note: The passage offers an evaluation: although it is somewhat luxurious, it would be difficult to maintain for long and may be suitable only for young people. Evidence for Question 4 concerning the overall content.
default.p.55new_n3-t31-p1.vietnamese:
People who have no home and live in places such as parks are called homeless people.

Because they have no money, they have no choice but to live in blue tents in parks or along rivers.

However, some people work for companies and can afford to pay rent, yet spend almost every night in a different place.

They are called "address hoppers."

Apparently, living this way costs less.

In addition, unexpected encounters are said to be one of the pleasures.

They put the necessities of life into a single backpack and move from place to place, staying at friends' homes, minpaku accommodations, share houses, and so on.

It is just like traveling.

Apparently, they use commercial services such as clothing rentals, luggage storage, and laundry services.

Because they have documents such as health insurance cards, they also have a registered permanent address, but in reality they do not live there.

In some respects, this lifestyle could be called luxurious, but it is difficult to imagine maintaining it forever.

Perhaps they can live this way only because they are still young.

default.p.55new_n3-t32-p1.outline.0.label: Introducing the “work-experience travel” trend
default.p.55new_n3-t32-p1.outline.0.note: Introduces a popular form of experiential tourism involving more than 160 occupations and gives its official name.
default.p.55new_n3-t32-p1.outline.1.label: Participants' purpose and motivation
default.p.55new_n3-t32-p1.outline.1.note: The reason working people participate is not to choose a career, but to try a dream job or an unusual occupation and find enjoyment in a new field.
default.p.55new_n3-t32-p1.outline.2.label: Tour features and opportunities to make friends
default.p.55new_n3-t32-p1.outline.2.note: The trip’s low-cost duration during the day, group size of 1–6 people, and possibility of maintaining lasting relationships after the trip.
default.p.55new_n3-t32-p1.outline.3.label: Applications in employee training and practical benefits
default.p.55new_n3-t32-p1.outline.3.note: The company applies it to employee training; the new experience provides contact with many people, refreshes one's perspective, and supports one's current work.
default.p.55new_n3-t32-p1.vietnamese:
Tours that allow participants to experience more than 160 different occupations are attracting a great deal of interest.

This type of tour is called 「job-experience tourism」.

Apparently, even people who already have stable jobs participate because they want to know what other kinds of work are like.

However, their purpose does not seem to be choosing a new career.

Many people reportedly want to try a job they dreamed of as children or experience occupations they rarely have a chance to encounter.

For anyone, being able to do something in a completely unfamiliar world is surely fascinating.

Most of the tours last only one day, so their low cost is also a major advantage.

In addition, the number of participants is limited to approximately 1 to 6 people.

When people go with others, both sides share an interest in the same job and perform the same tasks. Unlike ordinary travel, the relationship between them often continues afterward.

Some companies also use this type of tour for employee training.

Because participants do work that is completely different, they often have opportunities to meet people they have never encountered before.

As a result, their way of viewing things and their thinking gradually seem to change.

This is sometimes said to bring many benefits to their current jobs as well.

（Note）Training: Studying together to improve the abilities needed.

default.p.55new_n3-t33-p1.vietnamese:
City A has a population of about 30,000, yet as many as 620,000 tourists visit each year to experience agriculture.

Visitors can not only harvest seasonal vegetables and fruit, but also grow them themselves, naturally.

The area is very popular because it offers many activities the whole family can enjoy together, including a children's playground surrounded by nature, craft-making classes, restaurants, and vegetable stands.

Visitors can also spend the night in former elementary schools that are no longer in use.

City B offers baseball tours.

For just 13,000 yen per night's stay, participants can play against a volunteer team.

The facilities include a speed gun displaying the pitcher's throwing speed, an electronic scoreboard, a public-address system introducing the players, and an enthusiastic cheerleading squad.

As a result, participants can feel as though they have truly become professional baseball players.

The games may be won or lost, but interestingly, there is also a "hospitality" course that guarantees visitors a win.

It is said that about 20% of the teams choose this course.

When the program began in 2007, there were only 340 participants, but that number has now increased more than tenfold.

Good ideas are bringing local communities to life and making them more vibrant and developed.

(Endnote 1) Agricultural experience: growing vegetables and fruit or harvesting the products that have been grown.

(Endnote 2) Electronic scoreboard: here, a board that uses electric lights to display players' names and the score at a baseball stadium.

(Endnote 3) Player: a person selected to take part in a game.

(Endnote 4) Hospitality: making customers feel happy and comfortable in some way.

default.p.55new_n3-t34-p1.vietnamese:
“Mago wa yasashii” is a list of foods that are good for the body.

“Ma” refers to beans such as tofu and natto.

“Go” refers to sesame and other nuts and seeds.

“Wa” refers to seaweed such as wakame, kombu, and nori.

“Ya” refers to vegetables.

“Sa” refers to fish.

“Shi” refers to mushrooms such as shiitake.

“I” refers to root vegetables such as potatoes (Note 1).

Of course, it is good to eat the foods on this list.

However, it is not good to avoid meat and eggs simply because they are not on the list.

To build muscle (Note 2), you should also eat meat and eggs.

Whenever a food is said to be good for the body, people start eating only that food.

When another food is said to be good, that food suddenly disappears from supermarket shelves.

After a while, the craze dies down.

When something else is recommended, that item then sells extremely well.

This cycle repeats itself.

Even if you eat only foods said to be good for you, that does not necessarily mean you will be healthy.

I always think: why not eat a nutritionally balanced diet?

(Note 1) Root vegetables: potatoes, sweet potatoes, and so on.

(Note 2) Muscle: the parts of the body used when moving.

default.p.55new_n3-t35-p1.vietnamese:
Kanji were transmitted from China, but some kanji were also created in Japan.

In some cases, people did not know that a particular character already existed in China and created a similar one, or they used it with a different meaning from the Chinese meaning.

A famous example is the character “畑” (field for growing crops).

In China, both rice paddies and fields for growing vegetables are represented by the same character, “田,” but in Japan, rice paddies are written as “田,” while vegetable fields are written as “畑.”

It is said that people used to burn grass to clear land for crop fields, which led to the creation of this character by combining the fire radical 火 with 田.

For Japanese people, rice paddies (田) and crop fields (畑) are completely different things.

In China, the character “動” is used to express movement or activity, but the Japanese created the character “働く” (to work).

They thought that adding the “person” radical (人) to “動” would better express the idea of working.

The teaching of proper manners and etiquette is called “shitsuke.” People thought that combining “身” (body) and “美” (beauty) was especially appropriate, so they created “躾” (discipline)—a kanji that did not originally exist in China.

Because kanji can express meaning, the Japanese created many diverse kanji in this way.

I, too, have come to want to try creating kanji myself, just as people in the past did.

default.p.55new_n3-t36-p1.vietnamese:
Even if someone says “from 3 highs to 4 lows,” you probably would not understand what they mean.

This probably refers to the qualities women look for in a marriage partner.

Expressions such as “I would even carry a cooking pot” meaning that poverty would be acceptable as long as one could marry the man one loves have now become ①dead expressions (old words no one uses anymore).

The “3 highs” are ①tall height, ②high education, and ③high income.

① means being tall, ② means graduating from university or graduate school, and ③ means having a high income.

However, people say that today is the age of the “4 lows”: ④a humble attitude, ⑤low dependence, ⑥low risk, and ⑦low expense.

That is, ① not acting arrogantly, ⑤ taking care of one’s own responsibilities, ⑥ not creating worries about the risk of losing one’s job, and ⑦ not spending money on personal matters such as hobbies.

The “3 highs” belonged to a period when the economy was growing strongly. Apart from ②height, some young people may already have ③high incomes, but people who meet all the “4 lows” are extremely rare.

In particular, condition ⑦“low expense” may destroy men’s desire to marry.

Some people believe that if they have to give up their hobbies for marriage, it would be better not to marry.

However, these are merely wishes about how things would ideally be. From long ago until today, some people have wanted to marry someone who perfectly meets all the desirable conditions, while others have not cared much about them.

According to other data, standards such as ①kindness, ②thoughtfulness, and ③shared values—that is, feelings and ways of thinking, in other words, the heart—rank higher, while wealth, education, and occupation rank much lower.

③I felt a little reassured.

default.p.55new_n3-t37-p1.vietnamese:
It is said that cancellations without prior notice at restaurants account for about 1–3% of all reservations, causing losses of up to 200 billion yen per year.

This is because it is nearly impossible to require customers to pay cancellation fees.

Since customers do not feel that they must pay, stories sometimes make the news, such as customers being surprised when they are charged high cancellation fees, or students who cancel reservations without notice being exposed online and causing trouble for their universities.

Reasons for canceling reservations without notice include: ① “Making reservations at several restaurants at the same time to hold the spots.” ② “Carelessly forgetting that a reservation was made.” ③ “Making a temporary reservation because the restaurant is popular.”

If the idea that cancellation fees must be paid, as with airlines and hotels, became widely accepted, people might think more carefully before making reservations.

However, this is not a problem that can be solved immediately. (Therefore,) although it currently applies only to popular restaurants, a service has been created that allows members to make reservations as soon as someone cancels.

This business model is possible because these restaurants are all difficult to book and many members are ready to go at any time.

In addition, cancellation insurance for ordinary restaurants has also been introduced.

There are also services that collect the money on behalf of restaurants. Restaurants using these services must pay a fee equal to 30% of the amount recovered.

On the other hand, cancellations without notice lead to another difficult problem: (because) they cause a great deal of food to be thrown away.

For this reason, restaurants also factor these losses into their prices, so ultimately, canceling a reservation without notice does not benefit the customers themselves.

default.p.55new_n3-t38-p1.vietnamese:
People often say that walking 10,000 steps a day is good for one’s health, but apparently there is no scientific basis for the figure of 10,000 steps.

Surprisingly, it is said that a pedometer manufacturer came up with the figure of 10,000 steps in order to sell more products.

However, because walking is inherently good for the body, the idea spread widely before anyone knew it.

Walking 10,000 steps is quite demanding, and even if you walk slowly, it does not provide much benefit.

It is said that walking briskly for 10 minutes three times a day produces benefits equivalent to or greater than walking 10,000 steps.

Furthermore, even people who cannot manage to walk for 30 minutes a day can do a shorter workout that takes only about 2 minutes per week.

Sit on an exercise bike and pedal as hard as possible for 20 seconds.

Repeat this twice.

If done this way, the entire session, including a light warm-up beforehand and a cool-down afterward, will finish in about 10 minutes.

It is said that this workout is as effective as jogging for 45 minutes.

Furthermore, it only needs to be done three times a week.

When you do not have an exercise bike, after a light warm-up, do the following ①vigorous workout for 5 minutes.

The procedure is as follows: ① For 1 minute, open and close your arms and legs as many times as possible.

② For 1 minute, do as many squats as possible.

③ For 1 minute, remain in place and quickly raise and lower your legs as if running.

Then do exercises ② and ① again.

It takes only about 5 minutes, but it is very strenuous.

It is said that doing this set of exercises three times a week produces equivalent benefits.

I think this method is good for people who do not have much time.

However, taking a walk while chatting with friends is not a bad option either. (Nevertheless,) whichever exercise you choose, you should first check whether your health is in good condition.

Use the information presented here as a reference and try choosing an exercise that suits you.

default.p.55new_n3-t39-p1.outline.0.note: Pets are very important to elderly people, but they have shorter lifespans than humans, so their owners may die first and leave them without anyone to care for them.
default.p.55new_n3-t39-p1.outline.1.label: The wish to leave a legacy for pets
default.p.55new_n3-t39-p1.outline.1.note: Elderly people regard their pets as children and therefore wish to leave them inheritances, as is done in the United States; there has already been a case involving more than 100 million yen.
default.p.55new_n3-t39-p1.outline.2.label: Two legal solutions in Japan
default.p.55new_n3-t39-p1.outline.2.note: Because only people can inherit property in Japan, there are two options: a gift with obligations, 「前者」, and a testamentary trust, 「後者」.

default.p.55new_n3-t39-p1.vietnamese:
Pets such as dogs and cats bring their owners a sense of happiness, so they are very important to older people.

However, dogs live an average of 14.17 years and cats 14.82 years, so it is also common for owners to die before their pets.

As a result, it is not unusual for dogs and cats to suddenly lose their owners, go without food, become emaciated, or die.

Some people worry about this so much that they cannot pass away peacefully, while others are elderly and no longer dare to keep a pet even though they would like to.

This is especially true for elderly people who live alone: their pets are like their children, so naturally they want to think about their pets’ happiness.

Therefore, it is not strange that someone might want to leave an inheritance to a pet.

In the United States, it is possible to leave an inheritance to a pet, and one dog is said to have inherited more than 100 million yen.

Under Japanese law, only people can receive inheritances, so at present the only options are a “bequest with conditions” or a “testamentary trust.”

The former, a bequest with conditions, requires the recipient of the inheritance to do something in return.

In this case, the recipient would receive the inheritance in return for taking care of the pet.

The latter, a testamentary trust, involves entrusting the inheritance to someone else to manage.

That person would use the entrusted inheritance to pay for the pet’s expenses.

Since this method does not require the assets to be transferred directly to another person, the number of people using it will probably continue to increase.

However, simply using methods like these does not necessarily provide complete peace of mind.

The issue is whether it is possible to find a person or organization that will genuinely take good care of the pet.

There have been cases in which someone accepted the money without providing care, so another person or organization is also needed to inspect and supervise them.

If a reliable method becomes available, surely more elderly people will be able to continue keeping pets.

default.p.55new_n3-t40-p1.outline.1.label: The development of AI and the future of the Luddite movement
default.p.55new_n3-t40-p1.outline.1.note: The author predicts that AI will replace more than half of all jobs and explains why the Luddite movement will not break out again in the age of AI.

default.p.55new_n3-t40-p1.vietnamese:
In the 1910s, when the Industrial Revolution was advancing in Britain, the Luddite movement broke out.

Because machines began doing work that had previously been performed by people, workers who lost their jobs became angry and destroyed the machines.

Today, however, machines are manufacturing products in factories around the world. There are even factories with almost no people in them.

It is said that within the next 10 to 20 years, more than half of all jobs may be performed by AI instead of humans.

Although no one expects things to go quite that far, self-driving cars already exist, so surely that day will come eventually.

Not only manual labor but also intellectual work may disappear.

In that era, the Luddite movement will not occur either.

This is because even if a Luddite movement were launched somewhere, it would not occur everywhere. People in other places would continue implementing the technology, and in the end humans would still lose their jobs.

So what kind of work can only be done by humans?

AI is better at tasks such as collecting data and searching data for something.

AI can not only diagnose illnesses from data but can also decide on treatment methods.

It is said that even most lawyers will lose their jobs.

What should humans do? Surely people will feel anxious.

However, history teaches us that there is no need to worry too much, because new jobs are always created in every era.

As the amount of work done by AI increases, the amount of work done by humans will decrease, but work involving thought and reflection will certainly remain.

That is because AI cannot create something completely new in place of humans.

People will probably do creative work such as design.

Alternatively, it may become an era in which people can live simply by doing what they enjoy. Personally, I prefer the latter possibility.

default.p.55new_n3-t41-p1.outline.3.label: The real reasons instant noodles became popular worldwide
default.p.55new_n3-t41-p1.outline.3.note: Analyzes the key factors behind the product's success: convenience, requiring only boiling water; long-term storage; and the decision not to conceal the production method, which helped make noodles a global food with more than 100 billion servings annually.
default.p.55new_n3-t41-p1.vietnamese:
In 1958, instant noodles were first sold in Japan.

The first product was chicken-flavored noodles (Chicken Ramen), but after instant noodles began to be produced around the world, varieties suited to the tastes of people in each country were developed.

Spicy noodles are very popular in South Korea, while hot-and-sour flavors are popular in Thailand.

Exports from Japan reached 990 million servings and were shipped to as many as 50 countries worldwide.

Today, hundreds of varieties are produced in Asian countries, and some products are also exported to Japan.

China is currently the world’s largest consumer of instant noodles, but in per-capita terms, no country eats as many as South Korea.

This may be because South Korea began producing instant noodles shortly after Japan.

People often think that one reason noodles became popular was their low price, but when they were first introduced, they cost 35 yen. Considering that the starting salary for university graduates at the time was about 13,500 yen, they were by no means cheap.

Because they cost more than five times as much as udon noodles, instant noodles were very expensive then, unlike today.

Therefore, the reason they became popular was that anyone could prepare them immediately with only boiling water, and because they could be kept on hand, they could be cooked whenever people wanted.

In addition, because the preparation method was not kept secret, instant noodles gradually spread throughout the world.

By now, many instant-noodle companies have been established, and instant noodles have developed into a popular product, with 103.6 billion servings consumed worldwide each year.

default.p.55new_n3-t42-p1.outline.1.note: Explains how the brain processes two signals at once—pain and touch—and releases hormones that reduce pain and stress.

default.p.55new_n3-t42-p1.vietnamese:
When you were little, you may have fallen down, had someone say, “Pain, pain, go away,” and then (have them rub or touch the painful spot), after which you felt as though the pain had disappeared.

However, although we assume it is merely a feeling, apparently the pain really does decrease.

In fact, when we are touched, the brain has to receive not only the information “pain” but also the signal “I have been touched.”

Because it has to transmit two pieces of information at the same time, the transmission of pain sensations is reduced.

(In addition,) a hormone that relieves pain is also apparently released.

This hormone is also said to reduce stress and soothe and heal us.

That is why touching someone or being touched by someone helps us feel reassured when we are anxious.

The thing we touch does not necessarily have to be a person; an object can work as well.

This is probably ①why young children often hug stuffed animals or touch their blankets when they go to sleep.

That is why methods such as stuffed-animal therapy, doll therapy, and animal-assisted therapy are effective.

All of these therapies reduce anxiety through contact and touch.

A robot named Paro is one of these therapies.

Paro is very cute and soft, so when people see it, they instinctively want to touch and hug it.

It is also widely used in nursing homes.

Apparently, even elderly people who are normally irritable and give their caregivers a hard time become calm and gentle after touching Paro.

This shows that ②contact and touch have remarkably beneficial effects.

default.p.55new_n3-t43-p1.vietnamese:
In Japan, it is said that more than 5 million people aged 75 or older hold driver’s licenses.

Traffic accidents caused by elderly people are also increasing.

The number of traffic-accident deaths was highest in 1970, at 16,765, but fell to 3,215 last year.

However, it is said that more than 10% of those deaths were caused by accidents involving people aged 75 or older.

Currently, people aged 75 or older must take a driving-ability test, but it is clear that such testing is still insufficient.

This is because many elderly people have no problems during the test but cannot respond well when an unexpected incident suddenly occurs while they are driving.

Because it is dangerous, we strongly want them to stop driving, but very few of them actually do so.

One reason is that they still use their driver’s licenses as a form of identification.

Therefore, the police issue a "driving record certificate" showing the holder’s name and address as a replacement.

In addition, some cities offer half-price bus fares or discounted taxi fares to people who surrender their driver’s licenses.

Some places have even established a "paid volunteer transportation program."

Under this program, volunteers drive elderly people in their own cars. The transportation costs are inexpensive, and the driver receives a small payment.

Thanks to such measures, the number of people aged 75 or older who stop driving is gradually increasing.

However, when a car is their only means of transportation, they cannot stop driving even if they want to, because they need it for daily life.

I believe this is an issue the government must find a way to solve.

default.p.55new_n3-t44-p1.outline.0.note: An introduction to the HAL robot, which assists rehabilitation training for people with brain injuries, including how to wear it and why training is necessary.
default.p.55new_n3-t44-p1.outline.1.label: How HAL works
default.p.55new_n3-t44-p1.outline.1.note: Explains how HAL receives electrical signals from the brain through the skin, allowing a computer-controlled motor to move the legs according to the user's thoughts (Question 1).
default.p.55new_n3-t44-p1.outline.2.label: The effectiveness of rehabilitation training
default.p.55new_n3-t44-p1.outline.2.note: The brain relearns how to signal walking (Question 4); effectiveness varies from person to person (Questions 2 and 5), but everyone experiences great joy.
default.p.55new_n3-t44-p1.outline.3.label: Rental policies and corporate conscience

default.p.55new_n3-t44-p1.vietnamese:
The HAL robotic suit is a robot used for rehabilitation training.

It trains people who cannot walk because of brain disease or injury so that they can walk again.

First, electrode pads are attached, and then the 14-kilogram HAL suit is fitted onto the body.

Users reportedly do not feel that it is as heavy as that.

Wearing it does not mean that they can walk immediately; they still need to undergo training.

The intention to walk is converted into weak electrical signals and transmitted from the brain to the muscles.

Those electrical signals are also transmitted to the body's outer surface.

The electrode pads attached to the body receive the signals and send them to a computer.

The computer then sends the signals to a motor.

The motor moves the patient's legs, helping the patient walk.

HAL enables users to walk in accordance with their own thoughts.

Each time they practice, the sensation of being able to walk is fed back to the brain.

Through repeated training, the brain learns how to produce the signals necessary for walking, and the patient becomes able to walk independently.

Among the users, there are reportedly people whom doctors had told would definitely never walk again, yet after only four training sessions, their legs began moving 20 days later, they were able to stand the next day, and two months later they could walk on their own and were discharged from the hospital.

In terms of effectiveness, some people reportedly show very clear improvement, while others see little benefit.

However, even when they cannot walk, many people who previously could not stand are now able to stand, and this is bringing them great joy.

This remarkable HAL suit is reportedly available only for rental at present, and there are no plans to sell it on the market yet.

The reason is that research on HAL is still continuing, and the device is continually being improved into better versions.

Perhaps this is the conscience of the company that manufactures it.

default.p.55new_n3-t45-p1.vietnamese:
Almost everyone has heard of the Nobel Prize, but probably very few people know about the Ig Nobel Prize.

This prize was established in 1991 and is awarded for "research that first makes people laugh and then makes them think."

Whether the research is "useful to society" is not important.

Therefore, many strange studies receive this prize.

(There is no prize money, and recipients must pay their own travel expenses to attend the ceremony.) Even so, many people happily attend the award ceremony.

In fact, after winning the prize, many recipients reportedly gain opportunities to earn money, such as being invited to work as lecturers or speakers, but that is a result, not the original purpose.

The award ceremony begins by launching paper airplanes.

When a speech goes over 1 minute, a little girl walks up and says, "I’m bored to death. Please stop your speech," so the recipient has to give her candy or perform a trick to be allowed to continue speaking.

Many winners also participate with the attitude of "let’s make everyone laugh." (As a result), the award ceremony becomes lively, like a comedy show.

Many Japanese people have also won this prize.

Some inventions are quite famous, such as the dog-translating machine "Bow-lingual" and karaoke, but most of the research, such as studies on "the slipperiness of stepping on a banana peel," consists of topics that make ordinary people wonder why anyone would study such strange things.

However, I think that as long as Japanese people continue to receive this prize, Japan’s scientific ability remains entirely sound and continues to develop well.

That is because I believe that as long as society has enough leisure and prosperity to research even things that seem useless, its science remains strong.

default.p.55new_n3-t5-p1.vietnamese:
It is said that the world’s shortest letter consists only of “?” and “!”.

It was an exchange of letters between Victor Hugo and his publisher, meaning “Is it selling well?” and “It’s selling very well!”

There is something similar in Japan.

Expressions in dialect such as “Where are you going?”, “I’m going to take a hot bath!”, “Who is it?”, and “It’s me?” may be impossible to understand if you only hear them as they are, but it is interesting to think about what they mean.

“Sa” means a direction, “wa” means me, and “na” means you.

Thus, they become “Where are you going?”, “(I’m going to) the public bath,” “With whom?”, and “With you?” or “With me?”

Recently, there are also words such as “ri” and “ma?”

These mean “Got it (I understand)” and “Seriously? (Really?)” respectively, and young people are said to use them frequently in text messages.

Announcement of the Dondoyaki Festival

Dondoyaki is a "fire festival" held in many places throughout Japan.

It is an event where used New Year's decorations are collected and burned, while people warm themselves, roast and eat mochi, and pray for health and safety.

In Tozai City, this traditional event is held with the cooperation of volunteers.

Notice: Items other than New Year's decorations will not be accepted.

Please remove plastic parts from the decorations, as well as any other nonflammable materials.

Paper can easily be blown away and is dangerous, so it cannot be burned.

Schedule

Collection: 9:30 a.m.–1:30 p.m.

Lighting time: 12:30 p.m.

End time: Around 3:30 p.m.

Higashi Junior High School: Sunday, January 12

Nishi Junior High School: Sunday, January 12

Minami Junior High School: Sunday, January 19

Kita Junior High School: Sunday, January 19

default.q.55new_n3-t1-q1.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (a) ぐらい
Here, 「ぐらい」emphasizes the degree (“to such an extent”) and sets up the contrast in the following clause.
default.q.55new_n3-t1-q1.explanation: In N3 grammar,「ぐらい」can indicate not only an approximate amount but also a degree (“to the extent of”), emphasizing the limit of a situation. The sentence containing the blank is: 「私達はお世話になっている人の子供には多くあげ（ぐらい）が小さい子にたくさんお金をあげるのには反対だ。」. The complete meaning is: "We give a lot to the children of people who have helped us, but we oppose giving large amounts of money to small children." To avoid confusion, note the combinations:「だらけ」attaches only to nouns and describes a state full of undesirable things;「づらい」follows the ます-stem of a verb and means difficult to do; and「がちだ」describes a tendency to occur, usually negatively. Therefore, none of these three choices fits.
default.q.55new_n3-t1-q1.why.0: ✓ (a) Indicates degree (“to that extent”), emphasizing how much money was given and setting up the contrast in the following clause.
default.q.55new_n3-t1-q1.why.1: ✗ (b) 「だらけ」 follows a noun and means “full of” or “nothing but” negative things; the grammatical combination is completely incorrect.
default.q.55new_n3-t1-q1.why.2: ✗ (c) 「づらい」 follows the ます-stem of a verb and means "difficult to do something." It does not form a logical sentence with the following clause.

The key grammar pattern is 「Vてばかりいる」 (in the past, 「Vてばかりいた」). Following the te-form, it describes repeatedly or continuously doing something, usually with a negative, complaining, or critical nuance meaning “do nothing but...”. Here, the adverb 「決して」 and the negative ending 「〜のではない」 form 「決して〜てばかりいたのではない」, clarifying that the man did not become homeless because he was simply lazy. ✅ Correct answer: (a) って
The suffix 「って」 is the informal spoken form of 「という」 in the structure 「～ってことだ」 (= 「～ということだ」). It is used to report or explain the action of people from Osaka enthusiastically asking others for help when they do not know the way.

In everyday spoken Japanese, 「って」 is a shortened conversational form of the quotative particle 「と」 or the phrase 「という」. When it follows a verb in the plain form, 「Plain form + ってことだ」 is equivalent to 「～ということだ」 and is used informally to state or explain the nature of an action or event. The completed sentence means: “Even if that person does not know the way, they will still ask someone else for you, saying, ‘Does anyone know where XX is?’” As for the easily confused choices, the noun 「こと」 cannot follow 「みたい」 or 「よう」 directly; it requires the linking forms 「みたいなこと」 or 「ようなこと」, meaning something like or seemingly. The suffix 「っぽい」 also never combines with the dictionary-form verb 「聞いてくれる」. Therefore, only 「って」 is correct both grammatically and semantically.
default.q.55new_n3-t26-q1.why.0: ✓ (a) 「って」is the colloquial shortened form of 「という」in the structure 「～ってことだ」（＝ということだ）, used naturally and informally to quote and explain a situation.
default.q.55new_n3-t26-q1.why.1: ✗ (b) 「みたい」 expresses supposition or comparison. When it modifies the noun 「こと」, it must be used as 「みたいなこと」; it cannot be joined directly to 「ことだ」, and it does not fit the context of explaining an event.
default.q.55new_n3-t26-q1.why.2: ✗ (c) 「っぽい」 is a suffix meaning “seems” or “tends to,” and it follows a noun or the stem of a verb/adjective. It cannot follow the dictionary-form verb 「聞いてくれる」.

Grammatically, answer (d) uses the adverbial form of a na-adjective, 「反対な → 反対に」, followed by a verb such as 行う, together with 「今度は」 (this time; next), indicating a reverse sequence from the original order (①→②→③ becomes ②→①). In N3 reading-comprehension questions about procedures, the most common trap is answer (c), where learners may confuse the weekly frequency 「週に３回」 with the number of times the routine is repeated in one workout. Therefore, identifying the total duration correctly (five one-minute movements make five minutes) and understanding the broad expression 「反対に行う」 makes it easy to identify the correct answer.

default.q.55new_n3-t39-q1.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (a) たとえ
「たとえ」combines with the concessive ending 「～ても」to form the fixed grammar pattern 「たとえ～ても」, meaning “even if...” or “no matter how...”.
default.q.55new_n3-t39-q1.explanation: The ending sentence of the passage is:「安心できる方法があれば（たとえ）年を取ってもペットを飼い続ける人が増えるに違いない。」. The blank comes directly before the concessive predicate「年を取っても」. In JLPT N3 grammar, the adverb「たとえ」combines with「～ても／～でも」to form the hypothetical concessive pattern「たとえ～ても」. It emphasizes that even if an unfavorable circumstance occurs, the decision or result in the following clause will not change. The complete sentence means: "If there is a reliable method, the number of people who continue keeping pets even as they grow older will surely increase." To distinguish it from the easily confused「もしも」, note the following patterns:「もしも」combines with the regular hypothetical forms「～たら／～ば」, whereas「たとえ」must be followed by the counter-expectation forms「～ても／～でも」.
default.q.55new_n3-t39-q1.why.0: ✓ (a) It combines perfectly with the concessive conditional ending 「～ても」 in the following clause to form the familiar structure 「たとえ～ても」, meaning “even if...” or “no matter how...”.
default.q.55new_n3-t39-q1.why.1: ✗ (b) The adverb 「もしも」 expresses a hypothetical condition and usually accompanies 「～たら／～ば／～なら」 (“if”), not the concessive form 「～ても」.
default.q.55new_n3-t39-q1.why.2: ✗ (c) The connective 「それも」adds information or emphasizes degree, meaning “moreover” or “on top of that”; it is not an adverb modifying a hypothetical condition.
default.q.55new_n3-t39-q1.why.3: ✗ (d) The conjunction 「したがって」connects sentences expressing a cause-and-effect relationship (“therefore,” “consequently”), so it is not suitable before the conditional clause 「年を取っても」.
default.q.55new_n3-t39-q2.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (d) というわけではない
This expression means “it does not mean that...” or “it is not necessarily the case that....” It appropriately follows the contrastive conjunction 「しかしながら」 to reject the idea that using this method guarantees complete peace of mind.
default.q.55new_n3-t39-q2.explanation: The pattern 「Plain form (普) + というわけではない」 is an important N3 grammar pattern used for partial negation, meaning “it is not necessarily the case that...” or “that does not mean...” It often combines with 「～さえすれば」 to reject the one-sided idea that everything will be fine as long as one thing is done. The relevant sentence is: 「しかしながらこのような方法を取りさえすれば安心だ（というわけではない）。」 This means: “However, it does not mean that simply adopting this method will make everything safe.” This fits the following statement: 「問題は実際にペットの世話をきちんとやってくれる人や団体を見つけることができるかどうかである。」 (“The issue is whether it is possible to find a person or organization that will properly care for the pet.”) Remember the distinction between 「～わけだ」 (choice (a)), which expresses an explanation or inevitable conclusion, and the negative form 「～わけではない」 (choice (d)), which partially rejects a conclusion. Also avoid confusing these with 「～はずだ / はずがない」 (choices (b) and (c)), which express logical expectations or impossibility rather than negating a conditional claim.
default.q.55new_n3-t39-q2.why.0: ✗ (a) 「～というわけだ」 explains an obvious conclusion or summarizes a reason (“no wonder,” “that is why”), which is completely contrary to the contrastive relationship following 「しかしながら」.
default.q.55new_n3-t39-q2.why.1: ✗ (b) 「～はずだ」 expresses a confident judgment based on objective grounds, meaning “should certainly be...”. It does not fit a context in which the following passage points out a series of risks that make it impossible to feel reassured.
default.q.55new_n3-t39-q2.why.2: ✗ (c) Incorrect because 「～はずがない」 expresses absolute negation (“there is no way that...”), making the sentence illogical and contradictory when used with the conditional clause 「～さえすれば」.
default.q.55new_n3-t39-q2.why.3: ✓ (d) Correct because 「～というわけではない」 expresses partial negation (“it is not necessarily the case that…”), fitting perfectly with the contrastive transition 「しかしながら」 and the unresolved issue raised in the following sentence.

default.q.55new_n3-t39-q5.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (c) ペットに幸せに暮らしてほしい。
Pet owners, especially elderly people who live alone, regard their pets as children. Leaving them an inheritance therefore comes from the wish that they will continue to receive proper care and live happily after their owners die.
default.q.55new_n3-t39-q5.explanation: The strongest supporting evidence is the sentence:「特に一人暮らしの老人にとってペットは子供と同じだからペットの幸せを考えるのは当たり前だ。だからペットに遺産を残したい人がいても変ではない。」It means: "Especially for elderly people who live alone, pets are the same as children, so it is only natural to care about their happiness; therefore, it is not strange for someone to want to leave an inheritance to a pet." Choice (c) accurately expresses this wish using the important N3 pattern「V-てほしい」, formed with the te-form plus ほしい. The person whose action is desired is marked by the particle に, and the pattern expresses the speaker's strong wish that another person or being perform an action or remain in a desirable state, such as「幸せに暮らす」(live happily). In essence, elderly owners recognize that they may have shorter life expectancies than their pets and therefore want to leave assets through legal arrangements such as bequests with conditions or trusts, ensuring that funds remain available for the pets' proper care after the owners' deaths. In N3 reading comprehension, watch for traps that distort the author's meaning: choice (a) introduces a comparative「〜より」even though the passage uses the equal comparison「〜と同じ」, while choice (d) reverses who dies first. The passage clearly states that the owner dies first (「飼っていた人のほうが先に亡くなる」), not the pet.
default.q.55new_n3-t39-q5.why.0: ✗ (a) The passage says that pets are treated like children (子供と同じ); it does not compare them as more important than children (子供より大事).
default.q.55new_n3-t39-q5.why.1: ✗ (b) Owners always love their pets and hope for good things for them; they do not wish for their pets to die early.
default.q.55new_n3-t39-q5.why.2: ✓ (c) The owner regards the pet as a child, so naturally they worry about its happiness. This leads to the desire to leave an inheritance so that the pet can continue to live happily.
default.q.55new_n3-t39-q5.why.3: ✗ (d) The owner worries about the pet's safety after the owner dies first, not about what happens after the pet dies.
default.q.55new_n3-t39-q6.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (c) きちんと世話をする人が見つけられないこと
Although there are legal measures for leaving assets behind, the central and most difficult issue is whether a person or organization can actually be found to take proper care of the pet.
default.q.55new_n3-t39-q6.explanation: The direct basis for answering the question appears in the penultimate sentence of the passage: 「問題は実際にペットの世話をきちんとやってくれる人や団体を見つけることができるかどうかである。」, which means in full: "The problem is whether it is actually possible to find a person or organization that will properly care for the pets." Grammatically, the key structure 「〜かどうか」 follows the plain form (here combined with the potential expression 「見つけることができる」) and means "whether or not...," expressing a question or an uncertain condition. When used with the topic expression 「問題は〜」 at the beginning of the sentence, this pattern identifies the most difficult issue to be solved in a specific situation—in this case, ensuring the pets' lives after their owner's death. Many test takers may hesitate over choice (d) because the passage mentions that the owner's lifespan may be shorter than the pet's. However, that is merely the cause and background of the concern, not the central problem stated after 「問題は」. For this type of N3 reading-comprehension question, always follow transition markers and direct signpost expressions such as 「しかしながら」("however") and 「問題は」("the problem is...") to grasp the author's main point accurately instead of choosing background details introduced at the beginning of the passage.

default.q.55new_n3-t39-q6.why.2: ✓ (c) The passage states that the most fundamental issue today is whether a person or organization can actually be found to provide proper care for the pets.
default.q.55new_n3-t39-q6.why.3: ✗ (d) The owner dying before the pet is simply a fact about life expectancy that causes concern among elderly people. It is not the most difficult issue involved in protecting pets, as the question asks.
default.q.55new_n3-t4-q1.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (d) させていただきます
This is an official announcement from a store to its customers, so the writer should use the humble expression 「〜させていただきます」to politely ask permission to carry out the discount.
default.q.55new_n3-t4-q1.explanation: The announcement states: 「タバコ、商品券以外の全商品をミナミカードでお支払いの場合、銀行引き落とし（注）の時に10％引きと（させていただきます）。」 The party directly carrying out the discount is the store. The complete meaning is: "If you pay for all items except tobacco and gift certificates with a Minami Card, we will give you a 10% discount when the payment is withdrawn from your bank account." The pattern 「〜（さ）せていただきます」 combines the causative form with the humble expression 「いただく」. It is used when the speaker humbly and gratefully asks permission to perform an action that benefits the other person, and is especially common in Japanese service and business language. Distinguish the direction and subject of the action: 「されます」 is respectful toward the other person or passive, 「させます」 expresses making someone subordinate do something, and 「させられます」 expresses being forced to do something. Therefore, when a salesperson describes providing a service to a customer, the humble expression 「させていただきます」 is the grammatically and socially appropriate choice.
default.q.55new_n3-t4-q1.why.0: ✗ (a) This is incorrect because 「されます」is a passive or respectful form and cannot be used for an action actively carried out by the store itself.
default.q.55new_n3-t4-q1.why.1: ✗ (b) 「させます」is the causative form, carrying the nuance of forcing or allowing someone to do something, so it does not fit the context of a polite commercial announcement.
default.q.55new_n3-t4-q1.why.2: ✗ (c) 「させられます」is the causative-passive form, meaning being forced by someone else to do something against one’s will.
default.q.55new_n3-t4-q1.why.3: ✓ (d) This is correct because「させていただきます」is a formal humble expression used by the store to politely ask permission to provide the discount to the customer.

default.q.55new_n3-t40-q1.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (d) おそらく
The adverb 「おそらく」expresses a highly likely supposition and matches both the meaning and grammatical pairing with the sentence ending 「〜らしい」.
default.q.55new_n3-t40-q1.explanation: The sentence containing the blank is: 「今から10〜20年で（おそらく）半分以上の仕事を人間に代わってＡＩ（注１）がするようになるらしい。」. Grammatically, the adverb 「おそらく」 means “perhaps” or “probably.” It introduces a well-founded prediction with a fairly high degree of certainty and commonly pairs with predictive endings such as 「〜だろう」, 「〜らしい」, and 「〜にちがいない」.
